dockets.label: Rulemaking dockets
dockets.summary: One row per regulations.gov docket. A docket is the top-level folder a federal agency opens for a rulemaking or other action; it groups the documents the agency posts and the public comments it receives.
dockets.coverage: True range. Dockets as mirrored from regulations.gov, with modification dates from 2006-09-26 to 2026-09-06. The date records when a docket last changed, not when it opened, so it is a freshness axis rather than a coverage one.

columns.description: Unique docket identifier (e.g. `EPA-HQ-OAR-2021-0317`). Primary key / dedup key.
Posting agency's short code (e.g. `EPA`, `FDA`, `ACF`).
Human-readable docket title.
Docket category, typically `Rulemaking` or `Nonrulemaking`.
Timestamp the docket was last modified on regulations.gov (ISO 8601 string).
Agency-written summary of the docket (regulations.gov `dkAbstract`). Often null.
Regulation Identifier Number tying the docket to the Unified Agenda. Often null.

documents.label: Docket documents
documents.summary: One row per document posted to a docket — proposed rules, final rules, notices, supporting analyses, and public-submission stubs. Joins to `dockets` on `docket_id`. Two payload fields are not carried: `comment` (the inline submission body) and `restrictReasonType` (why a document is withheld). Read those from the acquisition source, the raw Mirrulations payload or spicy-docs' source-native release, not from this table.
documents.coverage: True range, floored. Posted dates are stated from 1990-01-01 to the present rather than from the raw minimum, which is the year 0000. See the data-quality note: the raw ends are a publisher defect, not coverage.
documents.data_quality: 52,699 rows (2.6%) carry a `posted_date` before 1990, including eight in the year 0000 and one dated in the future. These are publisher values carried through faithfully, not parse errors on our side. Filter on the date when recency matters.

columns.description: Unique document identifier. Primary key / dedup key.
Parent docket this document belongs to. Foreign key to `dockets.docket_id`.
Posting agency's short code.
Document title.
Document category (e.g. `Rule`, `Proposed Rule`, `Notice`, `Supporting & Related Material`).
Date the document was posted publicly (ISO 8601 string).
Timestamp the document was last modified (ISO 8601 string).
Start of the public comment period this document opens, if any. Often null.
End (deadline) of the public comment period, if any. Often null.
URL of the document's primary downloadable rendition. Retained for backward compatibility; see `attachments_json` for the full list. Often null.
JSON array of every downloadable rendition: `[{url, format, size}]`. Null when the document has no files.
Federal Register document number, when the document was published in the FR. Often null.
Whether the document was withdrawn, as the string `"true"`/`"false"`. Often null.
Agency-supplied reason for withdrawal, when withdrawn. Often null.
JSON array of additional Regulation Identifier Numbers beyond the docket's primary RIN. Often null.
Plain text extracted from the document's PDF attachment(s) by the PDF text-extraction step. Null until that step has run; see `text_extraction_status`.

Aggregate PDF outcome: `ok` means at least one PDF supplied text, even if another failed; otherwise `error`, `encrypted`, or `empty` (no extractable text) in that order. Null before an attempt. See `pdf_extraction_results_json` for each file.

Ordered JSON array from the latest PDF attempt: `{url, source_sha256, status, page_count, error}` per distinct selected URL. SHA-256 identifies observed bytes; no-bytes fetch failures have null digest/page count and a generic error. Null when no PDF attempt is recorded. Describes that attempt, not the provenance of older text retained after a failed overwrite.

comments.label: Public comments
comments.summary: One row per public comment submitted to a docket — the largest table (tens of millions of rows). On R2 it is also published as Hive-partitioned files under `comments/agency/agency_code=.../part-0.parquet`, one file per agency, rebuilt daily — this is what `spicy-regs-ui` reads for scoped queries. (An older `comments/agency_code=.../docket_id=.../year=.../month=...` tree was abandoned when comments moved onto the Iceberg catalog and carried a reduced set of columns; prefer the per-agency tree.) Joins to `dockets` on `docket_id`.
comments.coverage: True range, floored. Posted dates are stated from 1990-01-01 to 2026-09-06 rather than from the raw minimum of year 0000, on the same publisher defect as `documents`. See the data-quality note.
comments.data_quality: 33,373 rows carry a `posted_date` before 1990, the same publisher defect as `documents`. Filter on the date when recency matters.

columns.description: Unique comment identifier. Primary key / dedup key.
Docket the comment was submitted to. Foreign key to `dockets.docket_id`.
Receiving agency's short code.
Commenter's first name, when provided. Often null.
Commenter's last name, when provided. Often null.
Organization the commenter represents, when provided. Often null.
Submitter category as classified on regulations.gov. Often null.
Comment title / subject line.
Full free-text body of the comment. The largest field in the dataset.
Document category for the comment record, typically `Public Submission`.
Date the comment was posted publicly (ISO 8601 string).
Timestamp the comment was last modified (ISO 8601 string).
Date the agency received the comment (ISO 8601 string).
JSON array of any files attached to the comment: `[{title, formats:[{url, format, size}]}]`. Null when there are no attachments.

Plain text of the comment's attachment(s). Filled inline during the ETL from Mirrulations' pre-extracted text (the bucket's `derived-data` prefix); attachments not yet extracted upstream are backfilled by the on-demand PDF text-extraction step. Null when neither has produced text; see `text_extraction_status`.

Aggregate attachment outcome: `ok` means text was filled from derived-data or at least one PDF, even if another PDF failed; otherwise PDF outcomes prefer `error`, `encrypted`, then `empty`. Null before an attempt or derived-text fill.

Ordered JSON array from the latest PDF attempt: `{url, source_sha256, status, page_count, error}` per distinct selected URL. SHA-256 identifies observed bytes; no-bytes fetch failures have null digest/page count and a generic error. Null when no PDF attempt is recorded. Derived-data fills preserve these diagnostics; they do not describe the provenance of independently supplied or retained older text.

comments_index.label: Public comment counts
comments_index.summary: A tiny per-partition row-count index for the partitioned comments. It maps each `comments/` partition to its row count so consumers can compute comment totals and discover partitions without scanning the full comments dataset. Maintained by `update_comments_index`.
comments_index.coverage: Derived. Per-partition counts over `comments`; it covers exactly what that table covers and adds no rows of its own.

columns.description: Agency code of the partition (the `agency_code=` path segment).
Docket id of the partition (the `docket_id=` path segment).
Year of the partition, from `posted_date` (the `year=` path segment).
Month (1–12) of the partition (the `month=` path segment).
Number of comment rows in that partition file.

feed_summary.label: Docket summaries
feed_summary.summary: A pre-computed rollup with one row per docket, joining docket metadata to comment counts and comment-period dates. Powers feed/timeline views without scanning the full comments dataset. Built by `build_feed_summary`, sorted by `modify_date` descending.
feed_summary.coverage: Derived. One row per docket over `dockets`, `documents` and `comments`; it covers exactly what those cover.

columns.description: Docket identifier. One row per docket.
Posting agency's short code.
Docket title (from `dockets`).
Docket category (from `dockets`).
Docket last-modified timestamp; the table is sorted by this descending.
Docket abstract (from `dockets`). Often null.
Total comments on the docket, summed from `comments_index`. 0 when none.
Latest comment-period end date across the docket's documents. Null when unknown.
Earliest document `posted_date` on the docket, used as a creation date. Null when unknown.

agency_stats.label: Agency totals
agency_stats.summary: A per-agency dimension table — one row per agency with docket, document, and comment counts. Powers agency directory and profile pages. Built by `build_agency_rollups`, sorted by comment then document count descending.
agency_stats.coverage: Derived. Totals over `dockets`, `documents` and `comments`; it covers exactly what those cover.

columns.description: Agency short code. One row per agency.
Number of dockets posted by the agency.
Number of documents posted by the agency.
Total comments received by the agency, summed from `comments_index`.

agency_monthly_volume.label: Agency monthly volume
agency_monthly_volume.summary: Per-agency monthly document volume, broken out by document type — one row per (agency, year, month, document_type). Feeds activity sparklines and profile activity panels. Built by `build_agency_rollups` from document `posted_date`.
agency_monthly_volume.coverage: Derived. Monthly counts over `documents`; it covers exactly what that table covers, including its pre-1990 date defect.

columns.description: Agency short code.
Year of the documents, extracted from `posted_date`.
Month (1–12) of the documents, extracted from `posted_date`.
Document category counted in this bucket (e.g. `Rule`, `Notice`).
Number of documents the agency posted of that type in that month.

rulemaking_lifecycles.label: Rulemaking timelines
rulemaking_lifecycles.summary: Proposed→final rulemaking arcs, one row per docket, discriminated by `kind`: `pair` rows are completed rulemakings (earliest Proposed Rule matched to the earliest subsequent Rule in the same docket, with elapsed `days`); `stuck` rows are Proposed Rules with no matching Rule, where `final_date` and `days` are NULL. Bounded to `proposed_date >= 2010-01-01`. Built by `build_rulemaking_lifecycles` from `documents`. Note that pairing is per docket, so a docket carrying several RINs across successive rulemakings collapses to a single arc.
rulemaking_lifecycles.coverage: Derived. Proposed-to-final pairs over `documents`; it covers exactly what that table covers.

columns.description: `pair` (completed: proposed and final both present) or `stuck` (proposed with no final rule in the docket).
Docket the arc belongs to.
Agency short code, from the Proposed Rule.
Title of the Proposed Rule that opens the arc.
`posted_date` of the earliest Proposed Rule in the docket.
`posted_date` of the earliest Rule at or after `proposed_date`. NULL when `kind` is `stuck`.
Calendar days from `proposed_date` to `final_date`. NULL when `kind` is `stuck`.

fr_docket_links.label: Federal Register to docket links
fr_docket_links.summary: The Federal Register ↔ docket bridge: each `federal_register` row's `docket_ids_json` array exploded to one row per (docket_id, document_number, publication_date), carrying the FR display columns. Use this instead of an `ILIKE` scan over `federal_register.docket_ids_json` — it is sorted by `docket_id`, so `WHERE docket_id = ?` prunes row groups. This is the practical join from regulations.gov to the Federal Register, since `documents.fr_doc_num` is populated on only ~1% of rules. Built by `build_fr_docket_links`.
fr_docket_links.coverage: Derived, and bounded by its inputs. Links between `federal_register` and `dockets`, so it inherits the Federal Register table's 2000 floor: a rule published before 2000 has no link here because the document is not in that table.

columns.description: One docket ID extracted from the FR document's `docket_ids_json` array.
Literal Federal Register document number. Join to `federal_register` on both this value and `publication_date`; a number can name distinct dated records.
FR document title.
FR document abstract.
FR type: `Rule`, `Proposed Rule`, `Notice`, or `Presidential Document`.
FR subtype where the Federal Register supplies one, e.g. `Final Rule`, `Interim Final Rule`.
Date the document published in the Federal Register; required with `document_number` for the FR record join.
Date the rule takes effect, when the document carries one.
Comment period close date, when the document carries one.
Signing date, for presidential documents.
Federal Register agency slugs for the issuing agencies.
The full original docket-ID array, retained so consumers can see the other IDs this FR document links to.
RINs (JSON array) claimed by the FR document — the RIN-side join key for a rulemaking.
federalregister.gov HTML permalink.
Federal Register PDF URL.
Executive order number, for presidential documents.

discovery_signals.label: Agency activity spikes
discovery_signals.summary: Per-agency document-output spike signal that powers the feed's discovery panel — agencies whose document count in the trailing 30 days is at least 2× their prior-year monthly mean, requiring ≥24 documents in the prior year to suppress tiny-denominator noise. Recomputed relative to the run date, so rows turn over on every rebuild; it is a current-state signal, not a time series. Built by `build_discovery_signals` from `documents`.
discovery_signals.coverage: Not a range. A current-state signal recomputed relative to each run date, so every row turns over on every rebuild. It is not a time series and cannot be asked about the past.

columns.description: Agency short code.
Documents the agency posted in the trailing 30 days.
Prior-year monthly mean document count (months 2–13 back).
`recent_30d` divided by `baseline` — the spike multiple.

cfr_sections.label: Code of Federal Regulations sections
cfr_sections.summary: One row per Code of Federal Regulations *section* (a GovInfo CFR granule), ingested from the GovInfo API by `build_cfr_sections`. This is the codified, subject-organized body of federal regulations — `cfr_ref`/`title`/`part`/ `section` are the join keys back to Federal Register `cfr_references_json` and, transitively, to regulations.gov activity. Scope is section METADATA + CITATIONS only — the full regulatory *text* of each section is deliberately out of scope for this pass (it is far heavier). Requires an api.data.gov key (`DATA_GOV_API_KEY`); a keyless ingest run is a no-op. All columns are stored as VARCHAR. NOTE: the GovInfo traversal + field mapping await live validation with a key.
cfr_sections.coverage: Window. The 2025 and 2026 annual editions only, out of the Code's full publication history. This is the Code roughly as it stands now, not a record of how a section changed.

columns.description: GovInfo granule id for the section. Primary key / dedup key.
GovInfo package id (the enclosing CFR title-year edition) the granule belongs to.
Compact CFR citation composed from title/part/section (e.g. `40-60.1`). The join key to Federal Register `cfr_references_json`.
CFR title number (e.g. `40`).
CFR part number within the title (e.g. `60`).
CFR section number within the part (e.g. `1`). Often null for non-section granules.
Section heading / caption text as published by GovInfo.
GovInfo granule class / structural level (e.g. `SECTION`, `PART`, `APPENDIX`).
Annual CFR edition the granule was issued in (from GovInfo `editionYear`/`dateIssued`). Drives incremental freshness.
GovInfo last-modified timestamp for the granule. Drives incremental freshness alongside `edition_year`.
Canonical GovInfo details/link URL for the granule.

congress_bills.label: Congressional bills
congress_bills.summary: One row per bill or resolution. Two rollups write this table: `congress-bills` walks the Congress.gov list endpoint for the ten-column prefix across the whole archive, and `bill-family` fills the full contract for the Congresses it is scoped to — from a BILLSTATUS document for the 108th onward, and from the API bill detail route for the 82nd through the 107th, where no BILLSTATUS bulk exists. A consumer tells the two family routes apart by Congress and by the NULLs: a row for a Congress below the 108th is the detail route's, its `schema_version` is NULL because the detail record states no BILLSTATUS schema, and its `action_count`, `committee_count`, `version_count`, `subject_count`, `subjects_json`, `related_bill_count` and `related_bills_json` are NULL because the detail record states those only as sub-route counts the backfill does not walk — a zero would contradict the count the publisher declared. `cosponsor_count` is the one count the record does state, as its `cosponsors` sub-route's count, and is published from there (NULL when the record states no such sub-route, as the 92nd's do not). The BILLSTATUS route's separate count defect is described below. `stage` and `signed_date_rule` are NULL on these rows too: the record carries no actions, so no stage rule ran and no became-law action was looked for, and the shaper's default rung ("introduced") or the rule name "public law without a became-law action" would each be a statement about the bill that nothing examined. The first ten columns keep the exact order and spelling they have always had, because other repositories pin that prefix by digest; every new column is appended after them. Because two rollups write it, this is the one table merged column-wise: neither writer's NULL can erase the other's value. All columns are stored as VARCHAR.
congress_bills.coverage: True range on the archive index, mixed on enrichment. The earlier D1 output held 419,621 archive-index rows and enriched 18,956 bills of the 119th; its measured latest-action range was 1799-12-16 through 2026-09-18. The separate, bounded adoption validation covered only the 118th's HR and S BILLSTATUS archives: 16,213 bills, at 16 requests (8 keyed, 8 keyless), with four printing captures and no model calls. It recorded 1,368 populated CBO outcomes and 14,845 requested-empty:absent outcomes, with zero NULL outcomes in that local output. An absent element does not mean CBO never scored a bill. The first ten columns belong to the archive-index writer; all 39 appended columns belong to the bill family. Its own prior is re-read once where the CBO outcome is missing, even when the publisher stamp is unchanged. Receipt: `rollups-0-24-0-adoption-2026-09-20/`. Local output only; not uploaded.
congress_bills.data_quality: **Known BILLSTATUS count defect in vendored SpicyDocs 0.24.2:** the `cosponsor_count` description below incorrectly treats cosponsors as sponsors after the first. The publisher lists them separately. A direct native-XML audit found 13,154 wrong zero counts in the retained 118th Congress HR/S output. The corrected local SpicyDocs checkout and offline candidate count every listed cosponsor, including withdrawn entries, but the normal vendored package and prior outputs have not adopted that fix. Receipt: `legislative-release-candidate-2026-09-21/`. `statutes_at_large_cite` is filled at this table's merge by joining the published `laws` table on `bill_id`, as its column sentence says: whichever rollup writes this table (`congress-bills` or `bill-family`) reads `laws` best-effort after its own merge and takes the law's citation where one is published, keeping a citation already here where `laws` has none for the bill; with no `laws` table published the column stays as it was, NULL on a cold start. It is never guessed: `laws` publishes a citation only from a captured PLAW USLM file, and reads a NULL through its own `uslm_outcome`. `public_law_number` and `law_type` are not that case: they come from the bill's own publisher record — its `laws` entry, when the publisher states one — and are filled wherever the bill family has reached.

congress_bills.grain: One row per bill or resolution, as one BILLSTATUS document states it.

bill_subjects.label: Bill policy areas and legislative subjects
bill_subjects.summary: Subject assignments returned by Congress.gov or GovInfo BILLSTATUS, keyed by bill_id for a left join to congress_bills.bill_id. policy_area is one publisher category; subjects_json is a JSON array of legislative subject names, not separate bill records. The consumer trims and deduplicates names. All columns are VARCHAR, including subject_count. carrier and enriched_at record how and when the answer was obtained.
bill_subjects.coverage: Sampled. The retained table inspected on 2026-09-21 has 20,013 rows across Congresses 116–119; it is not a complete subject census. Each run selects pending bills from congress_bills, newest Congress first, with default caps of 2,000 Congress API or 5,000 GovInfo bills. Configured coverage floors are Congress 93 for the API and 108 for GovInfo. See docs/research/local-data-reuse-2026-09-21.md for the retained selection. These measurements do not establish current public availability.
bill_subjects.data_quality: A missing row can mean pending, failed or outside the configured scope. An empty assignment can mean no assignments or that the source did not hold the requested bill; those outcomes are not separately represented in this table. Retained same-carrier answers are not routinely refreshed. The table does not retain the original response or its digest.

columns.description: Stable bill key shared with congress_bills.bill_id, such as 119-hr-1. Primary/dedup key; join by this identifier rather than title.
Publisher policy-area name after trimming, or NULL when the returned answer has no policy area.
JSON array of trimmed, deduplicated legislative subject names. An empty array alone does not distinguish unassigned from not held.
Length of subjects_json, stored as a decimal string; not a count of bills or independent source responses.

bill_subjects.grain: One observed subject assignment per bill_id, with the latest retained answer replacing its predecessor.

unified_agenda.label: Planned agency actions
unified_agenda.summary: One row per Regulation Identifier Number (RIN) per agenda edition, ingested from the OIRA/OMB Unified Agenda published at reginfo.gov by `build_unified_agenda`. A Tier-1 rulemaking-lifecycle source: the upstream, forward-looking catalog of rulemakings agencies *plan* to pursue, keyed by the same `rin` that appears in `federal_register` (`regulation_id_numbers_json`). Primary / dedup key is (`rin`, `agenda_edition`). All columns are stored as VARCHAR; array-valued fields are JSON strings.
unified_agenda.coverage: Window. The 202510 edition alone, a single semiannual snapshot rather than a history of editions, so an agenda item cannot be compared against how it read in an earlier edition.

Short code of the agency that owns the RIN.
Full name of the agency that owns the RIN.
Title of the planned rulemaking.
Agency-written abstract describing the planned action. Often null.
Status of the RIN in this edition (e.g. `Active`, `Completed`, `Long-Term`).
Stage of the rulemaking in this edition (e.g. `Prerule`, `Proposed Rule`, `Final Rule`).
OIRA priority classification (e.g. `Economically Significant`, `Other Significant`, `Substantive, Nonsignificant`).
Semiannual agenda edition the row was published in, as `YYYYMM` (MM 04=Spring, 10=Fall). Half of the primary/dedup key.
Whether the action is a major rule, as reported by the agenda (e.g. `Yes`/`No`). Often null.
reginfo.gov publication identifier for this agenda entry, when present.
JSON array of timetable entries — the planned/actual milestone actions and their dates for the rulemaking.
JSON array of CFR citations affected by the rulemaking. The join key to the CFR.
JSON array of legal-authority citations the agency cites for the rulemaking.
Date of the earliest timetable action, when derivable. Often null.
Date of the next planned timetable action, when derivable. Often null.
URL of the entry's detail page on reginfo.gov.

federal_register.label: Federal Register documents
federal_register.summary: One row per dated Federal Register record, keyed by (`document_number`, `publication_date`), ingested from the federalregister.gov REST API by `build_federal_register`. The authoritative rule-publication record — proposed rules, final rules, and notices — complementary to the regulations.gov `dockets`/`documents` view. `regulation_id_numbers_json` (RIN) and `cfr_references_json` are the join keys to the Unified Agenda and the CFR. All columns are stored as VARCHAR; array-valued fields are JSON.
federal_register.coverage: True range, with a boundary worth stating. Documents published from 2000-01-03 to 2026-09-04. Federal Register documents published before 2000 are not in this table at all.
federal_register.data_quality: Document numbers are not globally unique: `00-111` names different records on 2000-01-14 and 2000-01-18. Current merging preserves both dates and replaces only the same dated record on a later successful fetch. This code correction does not restore historical records already lost from published files; those require a pinned historical replay and publication. A number-only source reference remains ambiguous when its input generation supplies multiple dated candidates.

columns.description: Literal FR document number (e.g. `2017-07442`); one component of the primary/dedup key with `publication_date`. Preserve its spelling.
Document title.
Agency-written abstract of the document. Often null.
FR category: `Rule`, `Proposed Rule`, `Notice`, or `Presidential Document`.
Date the document was published in the Federal Register (canonical YYYY-MM-DD). Primary/dedup key with `document_number`, and sort key.
Date the action takes effect, when stated. Often null.
Public comment deadline, for documents that open a comment period. Often null.
Date a presidential document was signed. Null for non-presidential documents.
JSON array of the issuing agencies as full FR agency objects (`raw_name`, `name`, `id`, `slug`, `parent_id`, …).
Comma-separated FR agency slugs derived from `agencies_json` (e.g. `transportation-department,federal-aviation-administration`).
JSON array of docket identifier strings referenced by the document (e.g. regulations.gov docket numbers). Joins to `dockets`/`documents` via `fr_docket_links`.
JSON array of Regulation Identifier Numbers (RINs). The join key to the Unified Agenda. Often `[]`.
JSON array of CFR citations as `{title, part, chapter, citation_url}` objects. The join key to the CFR.
URL of the document's HTML page on federalregister.gov.
URL of the document's PDF rendition.

This is the only body pointer this table carries, and it is the worse of the two the publisher offers: measured over 993 real documents, the HTML body carries publisher boilerplate on 993 of 993 and yields a median passage of 135 characters with 40.8% under 100, while the XML body carries it on 0 of 993 with a median of 610 and 6.8% fragments. org_committee_links.label: Commenter organizations matched to committees
org_committee_links.summary: One row per (commenter organization name, FEC committee) name match, derived by `build_org_committee_links`. Materializes the organization-name bridge between the regulations.gov corpus and `fec_committees` — the join the data model always described but left to each query author, so every consumer normalized names differently. `organization` is the raw string as filed, joining straight back to `comments.organization`; `committee_id` joins to `fec_committees`. Coverage is inherently small: `comments.organization` is populated on only ~0.08% of comments (~20.7K of ~25.8M), and most commenting organizations do not run a federal PAC, so a few hundred organizations resolving is the correct answer rather than a matcher to tune harder. Matching runs in three tiers (`exact`, `core`, `prefix`) and every row carries `match_method`, `confidence`, and `committee_match_count` so consumers pick their own precision bar instead of trusting an opaque score. A high `committee_match_count` can reflect multiple committees sharing a name prefix; inspect the source evidence before treating those matches as an affiliation network.
org_committee_links.coverage: Derived, and bounded by a small input. Name matches between commenter organizations and FEC committees, reachable only for the small share of comments that carry an `organization` value at all, so absence of a link is not evidence that a commenter has none.
org_committee_links.data_quality: These are heuristic name matches, not source-reported affiliations. confidence describes the matching rule, not a measured probability of accuracy. Matching names and resolvable committee IDs do not establish that the commenter and committee share an organization.

press_releases.coverage: Window. Measured on one run (receipt `d1-measured-run-2026-09-19/`): the two feeds were live with 10 House and 15 Senate items, and 5 of the 25 named one of the 18,906 bills held locally for the 119th. Each feed is a rotating window the publisher trims, so a single capture is only what was live that day; the table accumulates across runs and keeps every release ever captured. press_releases.data_quality: The bill linkage is a pattern match over the release's own words, not a publisher statement, so `matched_field` and `matched_text` carry what was matched and where: a false positive is readable from the row rather than only by re-running the matcher. One pattern is compiled per published bill in the Congresses in scope, bounded on both sides and built from the bill's own type, so a bare number matches nothing. Three states are distinct and must not be read as one: a `bill_id` with `match_rule = bill_number_in_title` or `bill_number_in_excerpt` is a match; `match_rule = unmatched` with a NULL `bill_id` means the matcher ran and no published bill was named; an all-NULL `match_rule` means no matching pass ran at all, because no `congress_bills` table was published when the rollup ran, or none was published for that release's Congress, or the release states no readable `pub_date` to scope by. The Senate feed carries no item description, so a Senate release can only ever match on its title. One consequence worth knowing before relying on these four columns: a run that cannot read `congress_bills` republishes the whole live window with NULL match columns, because this table merges row-wise and a fresh row wins whole. The next run that can read it re-derives them for every release still in the feed, so the gap normally lasts one cycle — but a release that rotates off the feed during that cycle keeps the NULL permanently. The other publisher columns are unaffected; only these four degrade.

roll_call_votes.summary: One row per roll call: the publisher's own tally, and the bill it refers to. The four tally columns are the publisher's own counts or they are NULL; they are never zero-filled. All columns are stored as VARCHAR.
roll_call_votes.coverage: Sampled, and accumulating. Measured on one cold-start run (receipt `d1-measured-run-2026-09-19/`): the `house-vote` index listed 676 House votes for the 119th, 577 of which the linkage rule could index, and all 577 were fetched from the Clerk under the 1,500-per-run cap with no refusal — 4 keyed and 577 keyless requests in 310 seconds, 577 rows produced locally from an empty prior. Local output only; not uploaded. House only, and bounded by that per-run cap on how many roll calls are fetched, newest first. A roll call already published with a tally is not fetched again, so a steady-state run is meant to read only new ones plus the newest few, which are re-read in case the publisher corrected them. **The skip is design, not measurement**: D1 was a cold start, so nothing was held and nothing was skipped, and the saving described here has not been observed yet — the second run is what measures it. The Senate's roll calls are not published at all rather than published with empty tallies — there is no Senate index route in the reader this rollup uses, and a set of Senate roll calls reached from bills is not an index of a session's roll calls. A House roll call that a bill's own action names can be published a cron before the Congress.gov vote index lists it, since the two linkage sources are read independently and the Clerk file is addressable from the roll-call key alone; such a row carries the same tally and member positions as any other, so this widens timeliness rather than the coverage claim. `vote_date` keeps the Clerk's own spelling (`9-Sep-2025`), which does not sort as a date, so no range over it is quoted here.
roll_call_votes.data_quality: The bill linkage has two publisher sources and `match_rule` says which one answered. `bill_action_recorded_vote` is a `recordedVotes` entry on the bill's own action, read from `bill_vote_references`; `house_vote_legislation` is the `house-vote` listing's own `legislationType`/`legislationNumber`. The first wins a disagreement, because a recorded vote sits on the bill's own action while the listing states a fact about the roll call from outside it. `conflict_count` is per roll call, not per run: it counts the later references that named a different bill for *this* roll call, and they are kept rather than dropped. `match_action_index` is set only on a recorded-vote match, since a listing reference sits on no action. With no bill-family run published, the listing linkage alone fills these columns.

table3_records.coverage: Sampled. Measured on one cold-start run (receipt `d1-measured-run-2026-09-19/`), and the measurement is mostly a refusal: of the 106 public acts the law route listed (108 laws, less the 2 private laws, which are not requested), 2 were read and produced 65 rows, 5 were refused, and the walk then stopped for the Congress with 99 acts unread — the per-run cap of 300 was never approached. An act already published is not re-read. **The skip is design, not measurement**: D1 was a cold start, so nothing was held and nothing was skipped, and the saving described here has not been observed yet — the second run is what measures it.
table3_records.data_quality:
Two things keep rows out of this table, and the measured run met the second far harder than the first. Table III lags enactment by tens of laws (the 119th stood at 119-73 there while the law route reached 119-110, measured 2026-09-14), and an act it does not yet hold answers a page cut off inside the site menu, which the reader refuses.
The second is the publisher's transport. On 2026-09-19 `uscode.house.gov` answered `GET /table3/{congress}_{n}.htm` with `200 OK` and its headers, then closed the connection partway through the chunked body: `httpx` raises `RemoteProtocolError: peer closed connection without sending complete message body (incomplete chunked read)`, which the acquirer reports as a transport failure after its three retries. It is invisible to a status-code check, because the status line is a clean `200` — all 20 attempts on the five failing acts (15 of them retries) returned one.
It is the publisher's and not the acquirer's, and it is a per-page truncation and not an outage. Both halves were re-derived outside the rollup with a plain `httpx.get`, no retries and no budget, against the same five acts plus one control act the same run had read whole: the five failed again and the control returned 63,493 bytes. The control is what carries the argument — five failures alone are equally consistent with the site being down. Retained as `table3-rederivation.json` in receipt `d1-measured-run-2026-09-19/`.
The rollup's two guards did their job and bounded the damage: each refused act was stepped past and left to the next run, and three consecutive refusals ended that Congress's walk, so the run spent 25 OLRC requests rather than 300 and stopped with 99 of the 106 public acts unread (108 laws listed, less the 2 private laws, which are never requested). Of the 2 acts that were read, 65 rows were published. A refused act holds nothing behind it and is retried next run, so the table fills as the publisher's body serving allows rather than failing the rollup.
An act's page is read once: a later edit to it (a status moving to repealed) is not picked up, and `release_point` says how current the captured page was. Private laws and pre-1957 session-law chapters are not requested. All columns are stored as VARCHAR.

budget_volumes.coverage: Sampled. The adoption walk served 40 BUDGET packages from the 2023-01-01 issue floor; all passed the thirteen-part provider grammar. It skipped 23 unchanged prior volumes and attempted the remaining 17 under the 40-package cap: six added rows and 11 root-format answers added none. The result holds 29 volumes. The six bodies contained 565 pages, all read, and produced 143 citations. The shared pass used 46 requests (38 keyed, 8 keyless). budget_volumes.data_quality:
**The bill counts are congress-blind and are not join keys.** A BUDGET package states no Congress anywhere — not in its id, not in its summary — so the print can only spell `HR7806` where the MODS states `119-hr-7806`. `distinct_bills` and `distinct_bills_beyond_index_congress_blind` therefore reduce **both** sides to `{bill_type}-{number}` before comparing, which is why the column carries `congress_blind` in its name; neither can join `congress_bills.bill_id`, which needs the Congress this family never states. For the same reason the per-row `stated_by_index` on a `bill_number` citation of a budget volume is **NULL, not `false`**: the comparison was not possible, and answering `false` would report a comparison nobody made. Measured across the eight volumes spicy-docs sampled at full page depth, 6 of the 8 distinct printed bills are print-only. The family's real yield is laws: **504 of 518** distinct public laws the prints name are absent from their own MODS at full page depth, against 43 of 69 at a 60-page cap. `fiscal_year` is not the issue year — `BUDGET-2026-MSR` was issued 2025-09-05 — and is stated twice, by the package id and by the MODS, which spicy-docs asserts agree. `associated_bills_json` is published whole because it is the only statement of this edge that carries a Congress.

**Thirteen measured parts are accepted by spicy-docs 0.24.0.** The seven additions are `OBJCLASS`, `TAB`, `DB`, `CLIMATE`, `LRB`, `CROSSCUT` and `DOD`. On one measured volume per part, `TAB`, `DB` and `CLIMATE` offer PDF only at granule stems; `LRB` offers an XLS and no supported body. A `GovInfoFormatNotOfferedError` at the package root is counted and logged as the publisher's answer, not as a failed or missing volume. No granule route is attempted: `shape_budget_volume` takes package summary/MODS and does not support a granule identity. bill_committee_actions.label: Committee-print bill actions
bill_committee_actions.summary: One row per action phrase a committee print states about one bill it names in the same sentence: the print's own phrasing, the sealed stage and BILLSTATUS action codes it maps to, and how reliable the pairing is. Joins `document_citations` through `document_key`, `text_sha256` and `mention_span_start` = `span_start`. All columns are stored as VARCHAR.
bill_committee_actions.coverage: Derived. The adoption run retained all 12,700 prior action rows and added none: all 41 accepted activity reports were unchanged. This output shares the print-citations pass's 46 requests, including 38 keyed, and package cap 40. It describes the matched activity reports, not all committee actions. Receipt: `rollups-0-24-0-adoption-2026-09-20/`. Local output only; not uploaded.
bill_committee_actions.data_quality: **These are rule-derived interpretations with measured errors.** `attachment_confidence` is `single` where the sentence names one bill and `multi` where it names several. Hand-checked over 60 mentions by spicy-docs: a `single` row is both the right kind of action and the right bill **83.3 percent** of the time (30 of 36), a `multi` row **50 percent** (2 of 4). `WHERE attachment_confidence = 'single'` selects the class with higher measured precision, at an 8 percent volume cost in that sample (4,089 of 4,456 rows were `single`). It does not qualify an individual row as correct. The vendored column description below still says "hosted-quality"; that wording is superseded by these limits and awaits adoption of the corrected source package. `multi` rows are kept rather than dropped because `sentence_start`, `sentence_end` and `matched_text` make them readable, and `bills_in_sentence` is published raw so a consumer can set its own threshold. **Precision is not recall: recall is 59.6 percent**, re-weighted by stratum over 148 checked contexts. The print writes "the bill" after naming it once, sets an en-bloc disposition as a sentence about "the measures", and states a committee consideration date in a ruled table's column header — so a consumer counting hearings from these rows is counting a floor. `sealed_stage` is **NULL on 1,670 of 4,456 rows** and that is a finding rather than a gap: a rung is never invented, so `passed the House` stays NULL rather than widening the sealed `passed house` matcher. `billstatus_action_code` is NULL on 280 rows whose phrasing has no known code at all (`vetoed`, `not_considered`, `declined_markup`, `favorably_forwarded`, `included_in`), and a further 639 rows are coded through codes the publisher's own retained guide never lists — 13 of the 35 distinct codes in the retained responses appear nowhere in its action-code table, which the guide itself says is representational rather than authoritative. `stated_date` is extracted and published but **was never scored**: nothing establishes that the date the sentence states belongs to this action. On a 20-bill probe the publisher had no counterpart at all to 10 of the 15 subcommittee hearings these prints state, while all 8 markups were stated and coded — which is what this table is for.

Character offset just past that sentence.

bill_committee_actions.grain: One row per action phrase a committee print states about one bill it names in the same sentence: the print's own phrasing, what it maps to, and how reliable the pairing is.

document_citations.label: Document citation link table
document_citations.summary: One row per occurrence of one cited key in one document's text: the key, the exact characters that named it, and the character span it was read at. Thirteen citation kinds, from bill numbers and public laws to RINs, agency dockets and GAO product ids. One shared link table over every document family, written by exactly one rollup. All columns are stored as VARCHAR.
document_citations.coverage: Derived. The adoption run added 143 citation rows from six newly admitted budget bodies and retained 49,935 rows after merging its own prior. All 41 activity reports were unchanged. The print-citations pass used 46 requests, 38 keyed, under the 40-package cap; eleven budget root refusals produced no citation rows. The two source families still have one writer. Receipt: `rollups-0-24-0-adoption-2026-09-20/`. Local output only; not uploaded.
document_citations.data_quality: **The span is in the identity because the span is the yield.** Keying on document, kind and target alone would collapse CRPT-118hrpt968's 267 bill mentions into 179 rows; the aggregate is derivable from this table with `GROUP BY document_key, cite_kind, target_key` and the reverse is not. **Different text digests retain their histories.** A source revision producing a new `text_sha256` adds findings beside earlier text versions. A successful rule correction for the same document and text digest replaces that digest's findings, including an empty result; it can retire obsolete rows. A failed read preserves previous findings. Size grows with retained text revisions and their citations. Filter to the digest the document row states (`house_activity_reports.text_sha256` or `budget_volumes.text_sha256`) to read exactly one extraction. Prints are revised rarely, so this is a property to know before building on the table; pruning earlier text digests would require a separate retention decision. `stated_by_index` is three-valued and the third value matters: `true`/`false` where a keyed index record was read and could state a key of this shape, and **NULL where no comparison was possible** — either no index record was supplied or the MODS vocabulary has no element of that shape, which is the case for every bill citation of a budget volume. So the consumer predicate for "what the print adds" is `WHERE stated_by_index IS NOT TRUE`, never `= false`. `target_resolved` false means the cite was found and its key is unsettled, not that the cite is wrong. `target_rule` says **how** a key was reached and separates lookups from inferences: `exact` and `roster_prefix` are lookups against a supplied vocabulary, while `name_prefix` and `sibling_prefix` are inferences from the printed text that a consumer may decline. `evidence_page` is NULL where the rendition states no page boundary, and a match straddling a page break is attributed to the page it began on.

columns.description: The citing document's own natural key in its family's spelling: the GovInfo `packageId` for a package, and one value per family as the table takes each one.
Which family the citing document belongs to, so one table serves all of them.

The cited key in the hosted target's own spelling, which is part of this row's identity: `congress_bills.bill_id` for a bill, the joined `laws` identity for a law, a committee's `system_code`.  Where nothing settled it, the rule's canonical form of the printed text stands instead and `target_resolved` says so, because an unsettled key is still evidence and dropping it would lose what only the print holds.

Character offset of the match in the document's normalized text, counted from zero.  Part of the identity: one document naming one bill forty times is forty rows, and the offset is what tells them apart.
Character offset just past the match, so `text[span_start:span_end]` is `matched_text`.
The printed page the match starts on, one-based, where the rendition states page boundaries; NULL where it states none.  A match straddling a page break is attributed to the page it began on.
The exact characters the rule matched, so a false positive is readable from the row without the document in hand.
Which table or publisher addresses the target key, as the rule names it.

Whether `target_key` is the hosted target's own spelling.  `false` means the rule found the cite but nothing settled the key: a bill with no stated Congress, or a committee name no supplied roster reaches.

How the key was reached.  The rule's own name for every kind but `committee_name`, where it is the resolution route: `exact` and `roster_prefix` are lookups in the roster vocabulary, while `name_prefix` and `sibling_prefix` are inferences from the printed text of this one document.  A consumer wanting only roster lookups filters on this column rather than on `target_resolved`.

Whether a keyed index record for this document already states this target key -- the package MODS's own `<bill>`, `<law>` and `<USCode>` section elements and its authoring committee.  NULL where no index record was supplied.  This is the owner's do-not-recreate rule, carried per row: where it is `true` the row's value is the evidence span, not the key, and `WHERE stated_by_index IS NOT TRUE` selects the kinds that are genuinely new.

Which rule in `interpretation/citations.py` fired.  Equal to `cite_kind` today, and a separate column because one kind can gain a second rule -- `interpretation/bill_signals.py` already runs two patterns for one bill number -- and the row must then say which one read it.

That rule's version, so a re-extraction under a corrected rule is attributable the way `prompt_version` is; the merge prefers the larger value.  Zero-padded decimal, because this column is compared as a string.
Which rendition the text was derived from (pdf, htm, xml, txt).
How that rendition became text (`pdf-extraction-gpo-normalized` for a print), which is what the offsets are offsets into.

Digest of the normalized text the offsets index into, and part of the identity.  A span means nothing without it -- a re-extraction that moved one character moves every offset after it -- and keying on it is what stops two extractions of the same document from colliding on one identity and silently merging.  The table is append-only per digest: a superseded extraction's rows are not retired, and a consumer filters to the digest `house_activity_reports.text_sha256` states for that document.

senate_expenditures.label: Secretary of the Senate expenditure tables
senate_expenditures.summary: One row per ruled row of one ruled table on one page of a Report of the Secretary of the Senate, with the cells exactly as the print states them and the roles its own header band names. Keyed on package, file, page, table, row and the page text's digest — the package id alone is not a key, because the publisher publishes the same printed pages as both a Full Report and a Part. All columns are stored as VARCHAR.
senate_expenditures.coverage: Sampled — the sample is a page window inside each file, and it was measured on one cold-start run 2026-09-20 (receipt `rollups-pdf-families-2026-09-20/`). The GovInfo `published` CDOC window from the 2024-01-01 issue floor served **291 rows and matched 5** Secretary-of-the-Senate reprints, and **all five were produced locally** — 3,272 ruled rows over ten granule files, zero refusals. It took two runs under the same 4-package cap: the first read four packages (2,623 rows, 640 pages, 556 tables, 21 keyed requests) and the second read the fifth, `GPO-CDOC-118sdoc11` (649 rows, 160 pages, 138 tables, 10 keyed requests), having found the other four already in its local prior and fetched no body for them. A package with nothing left to read costs its granule list and not a cap slot, which is what makes a window larger than the cap finish rather than stall. **Every count over this table is a floor on the volume**: each report runs 1,259 to 1,495 pages a file and only the first 80 of each are read, so `pages_capped` is `true` on all 3,272 rows. Those 80 pages carry the `A-` summary-of-transactions section and the start of the `B-` detailed statement; the `C-` compensation-of-members and `D-` mail-allocation sections the contents page names sit past page 2,000 and are not reached. These were local outputs, not uploaded; the documented public URL returned HTTP 404 in the 2026-09-21 publication audit.
senate_expenditures.data_quality: **Most rows carry one cell, not a row of cells, and `cells_ruled` is how you tell.** Of 227 ruled body rows across the 160 pages spicy-docs measured, the 56 in an `appropriation_summary` grid carry all nine cells and every other one carries exactly **one** cell of ten or of seven: the print rules a whole payee block as a single cell. That is why the contract has no `payee_name`, `document_number`, `date_posted` or singular `amount` column — those would be a parse of one cell's newlines presented as separate facts. `WHERE cells_ruled` selects the rows whose cells are separate facts; everything else is in `cells_json` exactly as printed. **`cells_json` is the row**; every other content column is a promotion out of it. `office`, `funding_year`, `appropriation_title` and `section_heading` are read from the page text and are **NULL on a continuation page**, which is 56 of the 139 measured table pages — forward-fill them in `printed_page` order. `printed_page`, not `page`, is what the report's own contents index by. `grid_kind` is NULL where the first row states none of the three known labels, so an unrecognised grid is visible rather than mislabelled. An amount must carry a decimal point to be parsed into `amounts_json`: without that rule a bare integer read stacked fiscal years and account numbers as money, and of 1,316 amount-shaped lines measured every one carries a `.dd` tail while the 143 that do not are all account numbers or fiscal years. The check that makes the extraction falsifiable is the print's own `Totals` row, which agreed to the cent with the sum of 28 account rows over seven money columns on both measured sections.

columns.description: The GovInfo package id the page belongs to, `GPO-CDOC-119sdoc3`.  Not unique on its own: one package publishes the whole report and each of its parts as separate PDFs, so `file_name` is in the identity beside it.

Which PDF of that package this page is in, `GPO-CDOC-119sdoc3-1.pdf`.  Part of the identity because the package's `Full Report` and `Part I` files carry the same printed pages -- measured byte-identical extracted text over the first 60 pages of GPO-CDOC-119sdoc3 -- and keying on the package alone would collide them.
The one-based PDF page the table was found on, as the extraction states it.

Which table on that page, zero-based, in the order the extraction returned them.  Measured 139 of 139 pages carry exactly one, so this is `0` throughout the sample and exists because nothing in the print guarantees it.
Which ruled row of that table, zero-based, top to bottom.

Digest of the page text this row's context was read from, and part of the identity.  A page, table and row ordinal mean nothing without it: a re-extraction that finds one more ruled band moves every ordinal after it, and keying on the digest is what stops two extractions of one page from colliding on one identity and silently merging.  It pins the text, not the table finder, so a change in the table finder alone is not visible here.

The print's own page label, the last non-empty line of the page text: `A-7`, `B-1243`, `x`.  Present on 139 of 139 measured table pages.  This is the locator the volume's table of contents indexes by; the PDF page number is not.
The section heading the page states, one of `SUMMARY OF TRANSACTIONS BY APPROPRIATIONS` or `DETAILED AND SUMMARY STATEMENT OF EXPENDITURES`.  NULL on a continuation page, which repeats neither.

Which of the print's three ruled grids this table is, decided by the label its own first row states: `appropriation_summary`, `organization_detail` or `payee_detail`.  NULL where the first row states none of the three, so an unrecognised grid is visible rather than mislabelled.
What the print makes this row: `header` where at least two of its cells are header labels, `total` where it is the grid's own `Totals` row or carries `ORGANIZATION TOTALS`, `entry` otherwise.

Whether the print rules this row into more than one cell.  `true` on every `appropriation_summary` body row (nine cells of nine) and `false` on every `organization_detail` and `payee_detail` entry row (one of ten, one of seven), so `WHERE cells_ruled` selects exactly the rows whose cells are separate facts rather than one block of text.

The office or account the page names above its `Funding Year` line, `SENATOR TIM KAINE`.  NULL on a continuation page, which the print leaves unlabelled; a consumer forward-fills in `printed_page` order.

The funding year the page's own `Funding Year` line states, and the **first** of them where it states a span, so a single-year block and a multi-year appropriation are comparable on this column.  NULL where the page states no funding-year line, which is every continuation page.

The last year of a multi-year appropriation, which the print spells `Funding Year 2021-2023` and its own contents spell `FY 21/23`.  NULL where the print states one year, so a span and a single year are told apart rather than folded together.  Five of the 83 measured office pages are spans -- the Chaplain's, printed B-48 to B-55.
The appropriation the page names under its funding year, joined to one line; the module docstring quotes one in full.  NULL where the page states none.

The first day of the period the table's own column headers state, as ISO `2024-10-01`.  Read from `FUNDS AVAILABLE AS OF October 1, 2024` or from the first date of a `PERIOD OF` header, the only two spellings measured; NULL where no header states one, which is every `payee_detail` table.
The last day of that period, as ISO `2025-03-31`, from `UNEXPENDED BALANCE AS OF March 31, 2025` or from the same header's second date.  NULL on the same terms as `period_start`.

One entry per column: the header label governing this row at that index, whitespace collapsed and exactly as the print spells it, or null where the band names none.  The band is the nearest run of header rows above this one, which is what makes the role correct in an `organization_detail` table -- it carries two bands, and column 0 goes from the office block to `DOCUMENT NO.` partway down.

One entry per column: the cell exactly as the print states it, newlines and all, or null where the extraction found no cell region there.  This is the row; every other content column is a promotion out of it and none replaces it.

The cell whose governing header is `APPROPRIATION TITLE`, which carries the account name with its fiscal years stacked under it, or `Totals` on the section's own total row.  Filled only where `cells_ruled`, so it is never a blob cell read as a title.

The cell whose governing header is `NO.`, the Senate's four-digit appropriation account number (`0100`, `4046`).  Filled on the same terms as `account_title`; the print states it empty on the `Totals` row.

One entry per column: null where the cell states no amount, otherwise every line of that cell that parses, in printed order, as objects carrying the exact printed line and its decimal.  A money cell stacks one amount per fiscal year, which is why this is a list and not a scalar, and a line that does not parse is not here and stands unchanged in `cells_json`.
How many amounts this row states across every column; `0` where it states none.
How many ruled rows the table this row belongs to has.
How many ruled columns it has.  Measured 7, 9 and 10 across the sample, one value per grid kind.
Left edge of the table's bounding box, in normalized displayed-page coordinates from a top-left origin.
Top edge of that box, on the same scale.
Right edge of that box, on the same scale.
Bottom edge of that box, on the same scale.
How many pages the whole PDF has, as the extraction states it: 1,335 and 1,264 on the two measured volumes.
How many pages the extraction actually read, which a bounded read makes smaller than `page_count`.
Whether the read stopped short of the document, so every count taken over these rows is a floor.
Which rendition the cells were read from; `pdf` for this family, which offers no other.
How that rendition became cells and text, as the caller states it: `pdf-extraction-lines` for the `NativeText` read these rows were measured on.
This module's rule version, so a re-extraction under a corrected rule is attributable; the merge prefers the larger value.  Zero-padded decimal, because the column is compared as a string.

bill_family_archives.summary: One row per BILLSTATUS bulk folder, holding the listing entry the next `bill-family` run compares against before downloading that folder's zip. All columns are stored as VARCHAR.
bill_family_archives.coverage: Not a range. The adoption run produced 2 rows in this output from the 118th Congress's HR and S BILLSTATUS archives, processing 16,213 bills in one pass. The chamber that took the roll call, lowercased (house, senate).
The numbered Congress the roll call belongs to.
The session number within that Congress, from the entry's sessionNumber.
The roll-call number within that session, from the entry's rollNumber.
Position of the action this entry sat on, in the publisher's own action order.

bill_family_backfills.label: Bill-family backfill state
bill_family_backfills.summary: One row per bill the pre-BILLSTATUS backfill has attempted, carrying the list stamp it was attempted under and whether it was filled or refused — the retained state that lets the next run retry every refusal and skip every filled bill for one comparison apiece. All columns are stored as VARCHAR.
bill_family_backfills.coverage: Not a range. The adoption run produced 0 rows in this output from the 118th Congress's HR and S BILLSTATUS archives, processing 16,213 bills in one pass. The pass used 16 requests (8 keyed, 8 keyless), with the printing cap fixed at four and model calls disabled. The pre-108th API backfill route was outside the declared scope. Receipt: `rollups-0-24-0-adoption-2026-09-20/`. Local output only; not uploaded.
bill_family_backfills.data_quality: A row with `refusal` NULL is a success record — the bill's `congress_bills` row is published and the stamp is what the `bill/{congress}/{type}` list stated when it was — and a row with `refusal` set is a recorded failure, which the next named run retries first, directly and without a list walk, one request each; that is the resume rule (the CRS summaries pattern: skip only a success, retry every failure). A list record whose stamp differs from its success row means the bill moved and is fetched again. The stamp is the publisher's own `updateDateIncludingText` exactly as the list stated it, compared as a string: an old Congress's list records truncate the instant to a date while its detail records do not, so only list-to-list comparison is exact. `refusal` is the error's class name only, never its message. All columns are stored as VARCHAR.

columns.description: The numbered Congress whose backfill walk attempted this bill.
The publisher's lowercase bill type (hr, s, hjres, sjres, hconres, sconres, hres, sres).
The bill's number as the list record states it.
The bill's `updateDateIncludingText` exactly as the list record stated it when this attempt was made; the value the next walk compares against.

NULL when the bill was filled; otherwise the class name of the error that refused the detail attempt (`_RetryableTransportError` after the reader's retries, `PagedJsonSourceError` for a refused response), which marks the row for retry.
When the detail request that filled the bill was captured, or when the refusal was recorded.

bill_family_backfill_walks.label: Bill-family backfill walks
bill_family_backfill_walks.summary: One row per (Congress, bill type) the pre-BILLSTATUS backfill walked, recording the route's declared total against what the walk reached and filled. All columns are stored as VARCHAR.
bill_family_backfill_walks.coverage: Not a range. The adoption run produced 0 rows in this output from the 118th Congress's HR and S BILLSTATUS archives, processing 16,213 bills in one pass. The pass used 16 requests (8 keyed, 8 keyless), with the printing cap fixed at four and model calls disabled. The pre-108th API backfill route was outside the declared scope. Receipt: `rollups-0-24-0-adoption-2026-09-20/`. Local output only; not uploaded.
bill_family_backfill_walks.data_quality: `list_completed` is true only when the walk reached the route's terminal page with declared and observed counts agreeing (the reader refuses otherwise); a run that hit the per-run cap mid-unit records how far it got and `list_completed` false, and the next run walks the unit again, pages charged to the cap, because only a walk can reach the records it did not. An empty success is not absence: `declared_count` is the route's own declared total for that query on that day, recorded beside `records_walked` even when the walk stopped early, so a capped walk can never read as an empty unit; a declared 0 is the publisher's statement that the Congress has no bills of that type. The declared total counts list entries, and the route can list one bill twice across a page boundary (`repeated_count`); whether that repeat also displaced another bill off the walk is not knowable from one walk, and a settled unit is not walked again to find out.
